prompt:
以下はある英語ニュースpodcast記事のFull Story・Point One・Point Twoです。
Point One・Point Twoそれぞれについて、以下6項目を判定してください
(それぞれPASS/FAIL)。

- qa_not_caveat_only: このPointが、研究上の限界・一般化上の注意・免責事項
  だけで構成されていない場合PASS(それらに加えて実質的な新しい内容がある
  場合もPASS。留保だけでPoint枠全体が終わっている場合はFAIL)
- qa_not_full_story_paraphrase: Full Storyの要約・言い換えに留まっていない
  場合PASS(Full Storyの中心的なlogic・結論を語彙だけ変えて繰り返している
  場合はFAIL)
- qa_not_other_point_paraphrase: もう一方のPointの要約・言い換えになって
  いない場合PASS
- qa_explains_why_it_matters: 「だから何なのか」を具体的に説明できている
  場合PASS(聞き手にとっての具体的な意味・示唆がある場合)
- qa_specific_not_generic: この記事のLedger固有の内容に基づいており、他の
  どんな記事にもほぼそのまま流用できる一般論になっていない場合PASS
- qa_adds_new_value: 新しい理解・解釈・意外性・具体的示唆のいずれかを
  実際に加えている場合PASS(Full Storyだけを聞いた場合と比べて、聞き手の
  理解が実際に深まっている場合)

reasoningには、判定理由を1〜2文の日本語で書いてください(特にFAILの場合は
具体的な理由を明記してください)。

【Full Story】
At first glance, Japan’s young travelers seem ready to slow down.

They want more control over their time. They want to follow their own interests. But there is a surprising gap between this wish and the length of their trips.

This pattern is especially clear among young men. In a survey, men aged 29 and under placed solo travel and hobby-focused travel among their top choices. About 25% chose solo travel, while a similar share chose travel that helps them enjoy a hobby more deeply.

A separate survey found a similar wish among Japanese Gen Z respondents aged 19 to 25. About 90% wanted free time during an overseas tour. Most of them wanted at least half a day of free time.

These results do not necessarily mean that young people want to stop visiting famous places. They suggest something more specific: many want to decide how they use their time, rather than follow a full schedule from morning to night.

But the numbers on actual travel plans tell a different story.

When people were asked how long they would travel if they could take one month off, “about one week” was the most common answer, at about 24%. Yet an autumn survey of people planning a trip found that their stays averaged only about 1.8 nights. The median was about two nights.

A 2025 tourism white paper also lists longer stays as an ongoing policy challenge.

So the change is not yet a complete move from sightseeing to long stays. The stronger conclusion is quieter: the wish for slower, more personal travel is growing, while actual trips are still short.

【Point One】
Here, slow travel may be less about counting nights and more about deciding what the hours are for. A short solo trip built around a hobby can still reflect that preference. The gender difference matters too: about 45% of women under 30 remain interested in visiting famous tourist sites. Flexible free-time blocks and solo-friendly choices may matter as much as longer packages.

【Point Two】
The one-week answer under a hypothetical month off shows interest, but it is not yet a normal travel pattern. The important question is whether bookings longer than about two nights become more common. For now, the evidence points to a strong wish that has not fully become everyday behavior. That leaves an unfinished opportunity for the travel market.
